enonce_markdown: In a categorical syllogism in standard form, which term is called the major term?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A standard categorical syllogism has three terms. The conclusion links the minor term (its subject) and the major term (its predicate); the middle term appears in both premises and never in the conclusion.

### Solution

The **major term** is the **predicate of the conclusion**. It is also the term which appears in the major premise, the premise which is stated first.

The subject of the conclusion is the minor term, and the term occurring in both premises but not in the conclusion is the middle term. The fourth option is not a way of defining any of the three terms.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The term which appears in both premises but not in the conclusion.
The term which has the greatest number of distributed occurrences.

enonce_markdown: Consider this syllogism: "No reptiles are mammals. All lizards are reptiles. Therefore, no lizards are mammals." What are its mood and figure?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The mood is the sequence of the types (A, E, I, O) of the major premise, the minor premise and the conclusion. The figure depends on the position of the middle term: figure 1 (M-P, S-M), figure 2 (P-M, S-M), figure 3 (M-P, M-S), figure 4 (P-M, M-S).

### Solution

Major term $P$ = mammals, minor term $S$ = lizards, middle term $M$ = reptiles.

- Major premise: "No reptiles are mammals" ($M$-$P$): **E**.
- Minor premise: "All lizards are reptiles" ($S$-$M$): **A**.
- Conclusion: "No lizards are mammals" ($S$-$P$): **E**.

The middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise: **figure 1**. The syllogism is **EAE-1**, the valid mood called **Celarent**.

EAE-2 would put the middle term as predicate of both premises, AEE-1 reverses the premises, and EEE-1 has two negative premises.

**Answer: A.**

enonce_markdown:
Which rule of the syllogism is broken by the following argument?

"All goats are animals with four legs. All dogs are animals with four legs. Therefore, all dogs are goats."
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Test an argument rule by rule. The middle term must be distributed at least once; a term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in its premise. In an A proposition only the subject is distributed; in an E both terms are; in an I neither; in an O only the predicate.

### Solution

Terms: major $P$ = goats, minor $S$ = dogs, middle $M$ = animals with four legs. Both premises are A propositions with $M$ as **predicate**, and the predicate of an A proposition is undistributed. So the middle term is **never distributed** in the premises: the rule of the **undistributed middle** is broken.

Other rules hold: "dogs" is distributed in the conclusion and in the minor premise (subject of an A), so there is no illicit minor; "goats" is undistributed in the conclusion (predicate of an A), so there is no illicit major; both premises are affirmative, so the rule on negative premises is respected.

The argument is **AAA in the second figure**, invalid: both dogs and goats are inside the class of four-legged animals without being related to each other.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The major term is distributed in the conclusion but not in the major premise (illicit major).
The minor term is distributed in the conclusion but not in the minor premise (illicit minor).
The middle term is not distributed in either premise (undistributed middle).

enonce_markdown: Examine the syllogism: "Some students are athletes. All athletes are disciplined persons. Therefore, some students are disciplined persons." Which statement is correct?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

To assess a syllogism, put it in standard form (major premise first), name its mood and figure, then check the rules: middle term distributed, no illicit process, no two negative or two particular premises, and the quality and quantity of the conclusion follow the premises.

### Solution

Terms: $S$ = students, $P$ = disciplined persons, $M$ = athletes.

- Major premise: "All athletes are disciplined persons" ($M$-$P$): **A**.
- Minor premise: "Some students are athletes" ($S$-$M$): **I**.
- Conclusion: "Some students are disciplined persons" ($S$-$P$): **I**.

Mood **AII**, figure 1 (**Darii**). The middle term "athletes" is the subject of the A premise, so it is distributed. No term is distributed in the conclusion (an I proposition), so there is no illicit process. There is one particular premise only, and the particular premise gives a particular conclusion. The argument is **valid**.

The three other options each name a fault which the argument does not have (it was also checked by exhaustive testing of all models).

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: It is invalid because the middle term is undistributed.
It is valid: it is AII in the first figure (Darii).
It is invalid because it has an illicit minor.
It is invalid because it has two particular premises.

enonce_markdown:
Put the following argument in standard form, name its mood and figure, and say whether it is valid. If it is invalid, name the rule broken and give a counter-example.

"No cats are dogs. All dogs are mammals. Therefore, no cats are mammals."
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Identify the major term (predicate of the conclusion), the minor term (subject of the conclusion) and the middle term, and write the major premise first. Then check distribution term by term: a term distributed in the conclusion must already be distributed in its premise.

### Solution

Major term $P$ = mammals, minor term $S$ = cats, middle term $M$ = dogs.

**Standard form.**

> All dogs are mammals. (All $M$ are $P$): A
> No cats are dogs. (No $S$ are $M$): E
> Therefore, no cats are mammals. (No $S$ are $P$): E

The middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise: figure 1. The mood is **AEE-1**.

**Validity.** The argument is **invalid**. The conclusion is an E proposition, so "mammals" is distributed in it; but in the major premise "mammals" is the predicate of an A proposition, so it is undistributed. The rule broken is **illicit major** (an illicit process of the major term).

**Counter-example.** Let dogs be mammals and cats be mammals too, with no cat being a dog. Both premises are true, but the conclusion is false: cats are mammals.

enonce_markdown:
Study the two syllogisms below. For each one, put it in standard form, give its mood and figure, test it against the rules and say whether it is valid. Name the valid mood if there is one.

(1) "Some drivers are not literate. All drivers are workers. Therefore, some workers are not literate."

(2) "Some workers are not literate. All drivers are workers. Therefore, some drivers are not literate."
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

For each argument, locate P (predicate of the conclusion), S (subject of the conclusion) and M, fix the figure from the position of M, then check the rules one by one: distributed middle, no illicit process, not two negatives, negative premise if and only if negative conclusion, particular premise gives particular conclusion.

### Solution

**(1)** $S$ = workers, $P$ = literate persons, $M$ = drivers.

> Some drivers are not literate. (Some $M$ are not $P$): O
> All drivers are workers. (All $M$ are $S$): A
> Therefore, some workers are not literate. (Some $S$ are not $P$): O

$M$ is the subject of both premises: **figure 3**, mood **OAO-3**. Check: the middle term "drivers" is the subject of the A premise, so it is distributed. "Literate" is distributed in the conclusion (predicate of an O) and in the major premise (predicate of an O). "Workers" is not distributed in the conclusion. There is one negative premise and a negative conclusion, and one particular premise with a particular conclusion. All rules are respected: the syllogism is **valid**, it is **Bocardo**.

**(2)** $S$ = drivers, $P$ = literate persons, $M$ = workers.

> Some workers are not literate. (Some $M$ are not $P$): O
> All drivers are workers. (All $S$ are $M$): A
> Therefore, some drivers are not literate. (Some $S$ are not $P$): O

$M$ is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor: **figure 1**, mood **OAO-1**. The middle term "workers" is the subject of a particular proposition (undistributed) and the predicate of an A (undistributed): it is never distributed. The rule of the **undistributed middle** is broken and the argument is **invalid** (there is no traditional name for it). Counter-example: let some workers be non-literate persons who are not drivers while every driver is literate; the premises are true and the conclusion is false.

The two arguments use the same three terms and nearly the same sentences, yet only the arrangement of the middle term (figure 3 against figure 1) decides the validity.
